PAGES.TITLE: Page Collections and Homepage Design
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The overview: what a page collection is, how it differs from a page, and how the homepage chooses what to show.
PAGES.BODY:
This page explains the design of page collections and the homepage together. It is the reason the two features work the way they do, and how they relate to each other on your site.

What Are Page Collections?

A blog is built around posts, which are dated and sorted by time. Many sites also have content that is not a post: a portfolio, a set of services, a set of guides. Those pages belong together, but they should not be dated or mixed in with the blog. A page collection is a themed index that links to two or more pages. It is a lightweight group with a title, a description, and a hero image, and nothing else. It has no body, no date, no author, and no comments, because those belong to the pages it links to.

How a Page Joins a Collection

A page joins a collection from the page's own editor, not from the collection. Saving a page replaces the whole list of collections that page belongs to. There is also an additive path, Add Pages to Collection, which adds pages to a collection without removing any existing membership. The page side is the source of truth, so a page always knows where it lives.

How Ordering Works

Members of a collection are listed by their sort order. New members go to the end. You can drag members into a new order in the collection's detail window, labeled Members (drag to reorder), and the new order is saved right away.

The Two-Page Minimum

A collection needs at least two pages before it appears anywhere on the site. The minimum drops to one when the collection has an external URL, because then it is a cross-link to another site and has no member pages to show. A collection below its minimum is not visible, and it is not selectable on the homepage.

When a collection falls under its minimum, for example because you removed a page, Galaxie Blog dissolves it automatically and shows an admin notice. Dissolving a collection does not delete the pages in it. The collection's address simply stops working, and there is no redirect, so check your links after a dissolve.

Hero Images and Enclosures on a Collection

A collection has a hero image. It also doubles as the collection's icon and its card image on listings. A plain hero image is the simplest option. A gradient is another option, and it replaces the hero image. A full enclosure, which can be an image or a video, is edited in the enclosure editor. Video is not offered for collections. When a collection has an enclosure such as a map or a carousel, that enclosure takes priority over the plain hero strings.

How the Homepage Uses Collections

The homepage can show three things, stacked in this order: a set of featured pages, a set of featured collections, and the recent blog posts. Each section is independent and additive, so you can turn on any combination. The homepage settings are saved together, and the save checks that every collection you picked is currently visible. If Pages is on, you must pick at least one page. If Collections is on, you must pick at least one collection.

One special case: if Pages is on and exactly one page is selected, that page's full content becomes the whole homepage. Use this for a landing page you want to control completely.

How the Homepage Is Cached

The homepage sections and the collection lists are cached for a day. Saving the homepage settings clears those caches, so changes show right away. If a change does not appear, use the refresh options in the admin, then see Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • A collection with fewer than two pages is hidden, and it will not appear on the homepage even if you pick it.
  • Dissolving a collection breaks its address. There is no redirect.
  • Page membership is set from the page. Saving a page can remove it from collections you did not touch, so check the page's collection list before saving.

PAGES.TITLE: Page Collections
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to create a page collection, add pages to it, give it a hero image or gradient, and feature a group of posts with a category link.
PAGES.BODY:
A page collection groups two or more pages under one themed card. This page covers how to create one, what it needs before it shows up, and how to style it.

What Is a Page Collection?

Visitors do not think in terms of single pages. They think in terms of "show me the portfolio" or "what services do you offer." A page collection matches that way of thinking. It groups the pages a visitor would look at together, gives the group its own landing page, and gives the homepage a single card to link to it. Creating a collection is the way to turn several pages into one section of your site, without building a new menu or a separate site.

Creating a Collection

Open Page Collections from the admin site and create a new collection. Give it a title and a description. The description is used on the card that represents the collection.

Adding Pages

Add a collection to a page in the page editor, using the collection selector. A page can belong to more than one collection. A collection is visible on the site only when it has at least two pages.

The Hero Image and Gradient

A collection's hero image is the picture on its card and at the top of its page. If you do not have an image, a gradient works too. The gradient editor lets you pick two or more colors, and an overlay text can sit on top of the hero.

Media for a Collection

A collection can show the same kinds of media as a post. In the collection editor, use the enclosure options to add one:

  • Image: a picture, cropped and optimized like a post image. See Adding an Image to a Post.
  • Video: an uploaded video, or an embedded one. See Video in a Post.
  • Map: a map. This needs an Azure Maps key. See Maps in Posts.
  • Carousel: a rotating set of images.

A collection can also use a gradient as its hero, with optional overlay text. Choose the media that suits the collection, then check its card on the homepage and on the collection's own page.

Featuring Posts

A collection's card can also point at a category, so the card links to the list of posts in that category. This gives a group of posts the same themed card a group of pages gets.

  1. Create a category, and assign the posts to it.
  2. Create a page collection with a title, a description, and a hero image.
  3. Set the collection's External URL to the category's listing link.
  4. Add one page to the collection. A collection with an external URL needs at least one page to show up, instead of two.

Clicking that card opens the category's post list, not a combined page.

Breadcrumbs

Breadcrumbs are the short trail near the top of a page that shows where the reader is. Page collections get breadcrumbs the same way categories do, and there is nothing to set up.

  • A collection's own page shows Home, then Blog, then the collection's title.
  • A page that belongs to a collection shows the collection's title after Home. A page in more than one collection shows each one.

On a phone, the trail on a collection's own page is not shown.

Gotchas

  • A collection with fewer than two pages is hidden, unless it has an external URL, which needs one page.
  • Posts cannot join a collection directly. Use a category with the external URL method above.

PAGES.TITLE: Configure Homepage
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to choose what the homepage shows: featured pages, featured collections, and the blog posts.
PAGES.BODY:
The Configure Homepage screen decides what visitors see first. This page walks through the choices, what each one does, and why the homepage is built from separate sections.

What Are Homepage Sections?

A homepage has to do several jobs at once. It should show your newest writing, point readers to your most important pages, and highlight a themed group of content. Galaxie Blog handles that by stacking three independent sections: Featured Pages, Featured Collections, and recent Blog Posts. Each section can be on or off, and each one has its own choices. You can run a blog-only homepage, a landing page with a few featured pages, or a mix of all three.

Opening the Screen

Open the admin site and choose Configure Homepage. The screen has a button labeled Manage Page Collections that opens the collection list, which is where you create and edit collections before you can feature them.

The Three Sections

Featured Pages

Turn on Pages, then pick the pages to feature. The list of pages is saved as a list of page IDs, and it can hold up to 500 characters of IDs. If you pick exactly one page, that page becomes the entire homepage, so think carefully before doing that.

Featured Collections

Turn on Collections, then pick the visible collections to feature. A collection has to have at least two pages, or one page when it has an external URL, before it is available here. If none are ready, the screen tells you that a collection needs at least two pages.

Blog Posts

Blog Posts is always on and cannot be turned off. It shows the recent posts in the number set by your entries-per-page setting, with a View All Posts link under them. Because it is always on, a homepage that only shows posts is the default.

How Saving Works

Saving checks your choices before it writes anything. It refuses a save if Pages is on with nothing picked, if Collections is on with nothing picked, or if any collection you picked is no longer visible. If the save succeeds, the homepage caches are cleared, so the new layout shows on the next visit.

A Plain-Language Summary

The screen shows a short description of what the homepage currently does, such as which sections are on and how many items each one has. Read that summary after each change. It is the quickest way to confirm the homepage matches what you meant.

How to Build a Good Homepage

  1. Create your page collections first, and make sure each one has its pages.
  2. Decide whether the homepage should lead with a landing page (Pages), a themed group (Collections), or your writing (Blog Posts).
  3. Turn on the sections you want, pick their contents, and save.
  4. Open the homepage on a phone and on a desktop, and check that the order makes sense on both.

Gotchas

  • Turning on Pages with nothing selected will not save. Pick a page first.
  • Picking exactly one page replaces the whole homepage. It is the most powerful option here, and the easiest to use by accident.
  • A collection can drop out of the choices if it falls under its minimum of pages. Check the collection list if a collection is missing.

PAGES.TITLE: Pods, Calendar, and Archive
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The small boxes in the sidebar: the calendar, the archives, recent posts and comments, and the other pods.
PAGES.BODY:
Pods are the small blocks in the sidebar. This page explains what each pod does, how to turn it on or off, and the reason the calendar and archive pods are built the way they are.

What Are Pods?

A sidebar lets a reader find their way around without going to a menu. Pods give you a set of ready-made blocks for the things readers look for most: recent posts, categories, the monthly archive, a calendar, and a way to subscribe. Each pod is independent, so you can use only the ones that help your readers.

The Pods You Can Use

The sidebar holds these pods, in this order:

  • Download is a sidebar block. Its text is set in its own section of Pod Content.
  • Subscribe invites readers to subscribe to new posts by email.
  • CfBlogs.org Feed aggregates posts from the CfBlogs community feed.
  • Pages lists your pages.
  • Page Collections lists the page collections featured on the homepage.
  • Recent Posts shows the latest posts.
  • Recent Comments shows the latest comments.
  • Category Archives lists your categories.
  • Monthly Archives lists posts by month.

The calendar is its own pod. It highlights every date that has a post, so a reader can click a day to see what was written.

Turning Pods On and Off

Each pod has an Enable checkbox. You find these on the Themes & Content screen, where each pod's settings sit beside its checkbox. A pod that is off is not drawn, and it costs nothing to leave it off.

Settings for each pod live with the pod. The Recent Posts pod, for example, has its own count, and the Download pod has its own text. Open the pod's section to change them.

How the Calendar Works

The calendar reads every date that has an active post and marks those days. That is why a calendar day can look different after you release a post. A new post appears on the calendar once it is released.

How the Archives Work

The Category Archives pod lists every category. The Monthly Archives pod lists posts grouped by month. Both are cached for a day, so a new post can take up to that long to appear in them unless the cache is cleared. Saving a post clears the archive caches for you, which is why most changes show right away.

How Pods Are Cached

Each pod is stored as a cached file. Saving a post clears the pod files that depend on it, including the archives, the recent posts, the recent comments, and the pages. If a pod still shows old content, reload the page first, then use the refresh options described in Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • A pod can be on but empty. The Page Collections pod, for example, stays empty until you have a visible collection.
  • Pods are cached. A change can take a moment to appear, so check after a refresh before assuming a problem.
  • Too many pods make the sidebar long. Keep the ones your readers use and turn off the rest.

PAGES.TITLE: Popular Posts and Related Blogs
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The scrolling strips of posts on the homepage and under a post: how they choose posts, and how to use the arrows.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog shows two lists of posts that help readers keep going: Popular Blogs on the front page, and Related Blogs at the end of each post. They do different jobs and are computed in different ways. This page explains both.

How Popular Posts and Related Blogs Differ

A reader who arrives on the front page wants to know what other people are reading, so Popular Blogs answers that question for the whole site. A reader who has just finished one post wants the next most relevant thing, so Related Blogs answers that question for one post. Splitting them keeps each list honest about what it is.

Popular Blogs

Popular Blogs appears on the front page only. Each post is scored by its view count divided by the number of months since it was posted, plus one. That formula favors posts that are both viewed and recent, so an old post with many views does not stay on top forever. The list shows the highest-scoring posts, up to twelve.

The list is cached for a day, separately for desktop and mobile views. Saving a post clears the cached copies of this list, so a new post appears once the cache is refreshed.

Related Blogs

Related Blogs appears at the bottom of each post. It is not computed from the content. Instead, it uses the related posts you choose by hand in the post editor, in the Related Posts box. The box shows the placeholder Select Related Post....

The relationship works in both directions. If Post A lists Post B as related, Post B also shows Post A on its own page. Only released posts appear to visitors who are not signed in, and removed posts never appear. Pages cannot have related posts, because they are not part of the post stream.

How to Choose Good Related Posts

Pick two or three posts that a reader would genuinely want next. Good pairs share a topic, a tool, or a question. Avoid adding every post on a theme, because a long list is harder to use than a short one. Since the relationship is two-way, a single choice gives both posts a link.

Gotchas

  • Related Blogs is manual. A new post will not appear in other posts' related lists until you add it.
  • Popular Blogs favors recent posts. A new post with a few views can outrank an older one, which is by design.
  • Removing a post removes it from both lists. Check the related posts of the posts that linked to it.

PAGES.TITLE: Configure Page Collections
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The admin screen that lists every page collection, its status, and its pages, with the tools to add pages, change the hero image, and set the order.
PAGES.BODY:
The Page Collections screen is where you create, arrange, and maintain collections. This page covers each part of it and the reason behind it, so you can manage collections without guessing.

Why Collections Have Their Own Screen

A collection is a group of pages, and it has its own title, hero, theme, and member list. Those settings are not part of any one page, so they live on a screen of their own. That keeps the page editor focused on writing, and it gives you one place to see every collection and its status.

Opening the Screen

Choose Page Collections from the admin menu. The screen lists every collection with its member count and status. Click a row to expand it in place, which shows the details without leaving the list.

Creating a Collection

Click + New Page Collection. The form asks for a title, a description, a hero image, and an optional external URL. An external URL turns the collection into a cross-link to another site. It drops the two-page minimum to one, and the link goes to that address instead of a collection page.

The collection's address is created from its title when you first save it. Changing the title later does not change the address, so the link stays stable.

The Collection Detail Window

Open a collection to edit its details. The fields are:

  • Hero Image (doubles as this collection's icon). The image shows at the top of the collection and on listings.
  • External URL. Makes this a cross-link to another site.
  • Theme. Sets the look of this collection's own listing view.
  • Members (drag to reorder). The list of pages in the collection, in display order.

An open link called open Pages jumps to the member pages, so you can add or remove members.

Adding Pages

You can add pages from the collection, using Add Pages to Collection. This adds the chosen pages to the end of the list without removing anything. You can also add a collection from the page's own editor, which is the other way a page joins one.

Deleting a Collection

Deleting asks you to confirm with Delete this page collection? Deleting a collection does not delete its pages. The pages stay where they are, and they simply stop being grouped. Remember that any link to the collection itself will stop working.

Gotchas

  • A collection under two pages is hidden, even if it exists.
  • The address is set from the title at creation. Renaming does not change it.
  • Deleting a collection breaks its address. There is no redirect.

PAGES.TITLE: Install and Admin, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The overview for installing Galaxie Blog, finding your way around the admin site, and configuring the blog.
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete path from nothing to a working blog: installing Galaxie Blog, signing in to the admin site, setting the blog up, and keeping it current. Read it once from start to finish, then use the links to go deeper on any step.

What You Need Before You Start

Galaxie Blog runs on a ColdFusion or Lucee server, and it stores its content in a database. You need three things before you begin:

  • A server running Adobe ColdFusion or Lucee. The blog is tested on current versions, and the install page lists exactly what has been tested.
  • A database that the server can reach. SQL Server, MySQL, and MariaDB are tested on current versions. Point the installer at an empty database, not one that already holds tables from another application.
  • The blog's files, downloaded as a zip. Uploading the zip and extracting it on the server is much faster than uploading thousands of small files one by one.

The reason for the empty database is simple. The installer creates its own tables, and it will not safely share a database with another application's tables.

Step 1: Put the Files on the Server

Upload the files to the folder your site uses. The blog can live at the root of the site, such as yoursite.com/, or in its own folder, such as yoursite.com/blog/. Either works. The installer does not ask you to edit any paths, because it works out where it is from where it lives.

If your host allows it, upload the zip and extract it on the server. That keeps the file count low and avoids a long, fragile upload.

Step 2: Run the Installer

Open the blog's address in a browser. If the blog is not installed yet, you land on the installer, which has four screens:

  1. Welcome. A short introduction, and a reminder to use an empty database.
  2. Site Info. The site's address and name. These appear in page titles, emails, and the feed.
  3. Database. The datasource name, the database type, and the connection details. You can also choose an existing datasource if you already set one up on the server.
  4. User Profile. The first administrator account. Use a strong password. It is salted and hashed before it is saved, so it is never stored as plain text.

When the last screen finishes, the installer creates the tables and the starter content, and signs you in to the admin site.

What the Installer Writes to Your Settings File

The installer records the datasource name and the database type in a small settings file, org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm, inside the blog's own folder. Because the settings live in the blog's folder, two blogs can run on the same server, each with its own file and its own database.

Step 3: Sign In and Look Around

Sign in at /admin. The home screen is a grid of icons, one for each part of the blog. Each icon opens in its own window, so you can keep several open at once. You only see the icons that your role allows. An author, for example, sees Create Post and Posts, but not Blog Settings or Users.

Start with three icons: Blog Settings, for the site's identity and connections, Blog Options, for the technical switches, and Create Post, so you can write something and see it appear. See Settings and Options, Explained and The Admin Site and User Management.

Step 4: Set Up the Blog

Set the basics before you publish anything. Work through these in order:

  • Blog Settings: the site name, the blog email address, the time zone, and the mail server. Email is how the blog sends comment notices, subscriber emails, and password resets, so set it early and send yourself a test.
  • Blog Options: SSL, the rewrite rule for clean links, the image and video limits, and the Azure Maps key if you plan to use maps.
  • Email and Comments: how the branded emails look, and whether you use the built-in comments or Disqus. See Email and Comments.
  • Clean links: if your server can hide index.cfm, set that up, then turn on the matching option. See URL Rewrites, Explained.

Step 5: Keep It Current

When a new version of Galaxie Blog comes out, upload the new files over the old ones. Then sign in and open Blog Updates. When an update is waiting, the icon says so. Each update shows what it changes before it runs, and the blog saves its progress after each step, so a failed update can be started again. See An Installer That Updates Itself.

After you upload files, restart the application server, not just the blog. The server remembers old code until it restarts, and a reinitialize does not always clear it.

When Something Goes Wrong

Most problems fall into three groups. A page that will not load usually means the database or the datasource is wrong, so check the settings file and the datasource in your server's administrator. A change that does not appear usually means a stale cache, so reinitialize or use Refresh Site. A startup error that the visitor cannot see is written to the galaxieBlogErrors log on the server. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Where to Go Next

  • Installing Galaxie Blog 4.66: the installer screen by screen.
  • The Admin Site and User Management: roles, capabilities, and the user tools.
  • Post Editing, Start to Finish: writing your first post.

Gotchas

  • Use an empty database. A database with other tables in it can cause the installer to fail partway.
  • Send yourself a test email early. A mail problem found on day one is much easier to fix than one found the day a post goes out.
  • Restart after moving files. A reinitialize alone can leave old code running.

See Also

  • Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs
  • Search Engines and Feeds

PAGES.TITLE: Installing Galaxie Blog 4.66
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Installing Galaxie Blog 4.66
PAGES.BODY:
If you're installing Galaxie Blog for the first time, this walks through it end to end. It installs itself through a short four-screen wizard, with nothing to edit by hand along the way.

Before You Start

Your server needs one of these:

  • Adobe ColdFusion. I develop on ColdFusion 2025 and have also tested on 2023; earlier versions back to 2018 have worked for other users, but I have not personally tested 2016.
  • Lucee. I develop and test on Lucee 7.1, and it also runs on Lucee 6.2.

You also need a database: Galaxie Blog uses the database support built into Adobe ColdFusion or Lucee. Check their current lists for the latest. Tested here: SQL Server, MySQL, and MariaDB on current versions, and PostgreSQL and Oracle on older versions. Try a fresh install on a copy before you use another database. See Adobe's ORM settings for the full list of database dialects that ColdFusion supports. The ORM handles the few database-specific column types (see the Gotchas section). You do not need to create the database tables yourself, and you should point the installer at an empty database, not one with existing tables from something else, to avoid a conflict.

Download and Extract

Download the current Galaxie Blog zip file and extract it. Uploading it to your server as a zip and extracting it there, if your host allows that, is much faster than uploading thousands of small files one at a time over FTP.

Upload to the Server

Upload the extracted files to your server. Galaxie Blog can live at the root of a site, or in its own folder such as /blog, and it does not need a datasource with a special reserved name: the installer creates or reuses whatever datasource name you tell it to, and writes that name into org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm in the blog's own folder. This also means you can run more than one blog on the same server, each in its own folder with its own ini file and its own datasource.

Running the Installer (4 Steps)

Open the blog's address in a browser. If it is not yet installed, you land on the installer.

  • Step 1 of 4, Welcome. A short introduction and the same empty-database note as above.
  • Step 2 of 4, Site Info. The site's URL and name.
  • Step 3 of 4, Database. The datasource name, and the database vendor and connection details (or an existing datasource, if you already created one on the server).
  • Step 4 of 4, User Profile. Your administrator account: name, email and password. The password is salted and hashed before it's saved, never stored in plain text or in a reversible form.

The installer then builds the database tables and starter data, and signs you in to the admin interface.

Updating an Existing Blog

This article covers a new install. If you already have a Galaxie Blog and are bringing it up to 4.66 from an older version, that's a different process: upload the new files over the old ones, then use the Blog Updates screen in the admin interface, which runs the database update for you. The full steps, and the changes in each version, are in UPGRADING.md in the project's repository.

Gotchas

  • The blog only shows the real startup error if you add ?startupDebug=1 to the address, and you are signed in as an administrator (or the blog is not installed yet). Otherwise, only a generic message is shown, and the real error is written to the galaxieBlogErrors log on the server.
  • Restart, or clear the caches, after moving or deleting files. Both ColdFusion and Lucee remember where they found a component and the database mapping, and stale ones can cause confusing errors after you rearrange files on the server.
  • Long text columns are handled for you. Every database vendor names its "long text" column type differently. On first start, DatabaseOrmTypes.cfc rewrites the handful of ORM entities that need one (the post body, comments and similar) to match the database type you chose in the installer. You do not need to copy in different files for different databases.
  • .webp and .vtt need a mime type on IIS. The web.config that ships with Galaxie Blog already adds both, for the image format the media library uses and for video captions.

PAGES.TITLE: Updating Galaxie Blog
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How Galaxie Blog installs and updates itself, so you never edit files by hand for an upgrade.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog does not update its own files. Nothing downloads new code while the blog runs. Updating is a two-part job: you put the new files on the server, then you run a database update from inside the admin site. This page explains why the update works that way, and what each part does.

Why Files and the Database Are Updated Separately

The code is the set of files the site runs on. The database holds your posts, settings, and users. A new release can change either or both. Keeping the file upload and the database update as separate steps means you can see what changed before you run it, and you can stop if something looks wrong. A blog that rewrote its own code in the background would make that check impossible.

Step 1: Put the Files on the Server

Upload the new release's files to your server, replacing the old ones. Do not overwrite your blog's configuration file, org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm, since it holds your database connection. The admin's update check repeats this warning.

Step 2: Check for a New Version

The latestVersionCheck screen reads a version feed and lists every release newer than the one you have installed. For each release it shows the notes, the bug fixes, and the files changed. It only reads and displays the information. It does not download anything, so you still upload the files yourself.

Step 3: Run the Database Update

Open Blog Updates in the admin site and click Update Galaxie Blog's database. The update runs the version scripts in order. Each script is tied to a release, and the blog saves its version after each one. If a script fails, the run stops there, so you can fix the problem and run the update again without repeating the steps that already worked.

If your database is too old to use the admin site, the blog sends you to a standalone update page instead. That page has the same button and the same behavior.

What Visitors See During an Update

The blog will not run against a database that is too old for the current code. Until the update finishes, visitors see a page saying the site is being updated, and administrators are sent to the update page. This protects visitors from errors caused by a half-updated database.

Gotchas

  • Upload the files first, then run the database update. Running it against old files will not work.
  • Do not overwrite the configuration file. Your database connection lives there.
  • The update check does not download code. It only tells you what is new.

PAGES.TITLE: The Admin Site and User Management
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The admin home screen, the icons you see for your role, and how to add users, set roles and capabilities, and handle logins and bans.
PAGES.BODY:
The admin interface is where you manage posts, pages, media, users, comments, themes, and server settings. This page covers the home screen and the user tools.

Getting There

Sign in at /admin. The home screen is a grid of icons, and each one opens in a window over the same page, so you can have several open at once.

The Icons

For an administrator the icons include Create Post, Pages, Posts, Comments, Categories, Tags, Fonts, Subscribers, Users, User Profile, Themes and Content, Blog Settings, Blog Options, Visitor Log, Ban Visitors, Banned Users, Admin Log, Error Log, Reaction Log, Search Queries, Import Data, Blog Updates, Refresh Site, and Reload ORM Objects.

The Blog Updates icon shows "(update needed)" when the database is behind the blog's version. See An Installer That Updates Itself.

What You See Depends on Your Role

You only see the icons your role or capabilities allow. An Author, for example, sees Create Post and Posts, but not Blog Settings or Users.

Roles

  • Administrator: everything.
  • SuperUser: everything except server and database settings.
  • Author: create and edit their own posts.
  • Editor: edit and make posts, and adjust categories and related posts.
  • Designer: edit theme settings, and add images to posts.
  • Moderator: edit or remove comments, and ban users.
  • Subscriber: upload photos in their own comments, and edit their own profile.
  • Guest: view posts and comment, without uploading media.

You can also give a user individual capabilities, or build a custom role. The capabilities include Create Post, Manage Images, Manage Categories, Manage Comments, Manage Files, Manage Pages, Edit Posts, Edit User Profile, Manage Settings, Manage Subscribers, Manage Templates, Manage Themes, Manage Users, and Schedule and Release Posts.

Adding a User

Click Create New User at the top of the User grid. Every field except the website is required, and the user name must be unique. The password you enter is only used for their first sign-in. A branded email then asks them to finish their profile and choose their own password.

Passwords and Login History

Passwords are salted and hashed before they are saved, so nobody can look one up, including an administrator. A user who forgets their password needs their own access to change it from their profile. To see a user's logins, open their profile and click Login History.

Bans

Ban Visitors bans by IP address or by User-Agent. Banned Users lists who is banned, when, and by whom. Both need the Manage Users capability.

Gotchas

  • Passwords cannot be recovered. Plan support around that.
  • Invite links do not expire. Treat an unused invite like any other credential.
  • Guest and Subscriber are working roles. Guests can comment, and Subscribers can also comment with photos.

PAGES.TITLE: Settings and Options, Explained
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Blog Settings for the site identity and connections, and Blog Options for the technical switches, panels, and API keys.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog has two places for configuration, and they answer different questions. Blog Settings describes who the blog is and how it connects to the outside world. Blog Options controls how the blog behaves. This page walks through both screens, explains why each setting exists, and tells you what to check when you change one.

Blog Options vs Blog Settings

Settings are about identity and connections: your name, your time zone, your database, and your mail server. These change rarely, and a mistake can stop the blog from working, so they sit on their own screen. Options are about behavior: caching, minifying, limits, and third-party libraries. These change more often, and most take effect as soon as you save them.

Blog Settings, Step by Step

Open Blog Settings from the admin home screen. The main block is at the top, followed by four collapsible panels.

The Main Block

  • Site name and blog email. The name appears in titles and emails. The email is the sender for the blog's messages.
  • Production Site. Leave this unchecked while you build or test the blog, so a staging copy is not indexed by search engines by mistake. Check it when you go live.

Parent Site

If your blog sits under a larger site, enter that site's name and address here. The blog uses them to link back to the parent site from its menu.

Server Time Zone

Set the time zone the server runs in. Post dates, release times, and scheduled posts all use it. A post set for 9 a.m. goes out at 9 a.m. on the server's clock, so check it if your server is in another zone.

Database Connectivity

The datasource name, user name, and password are saved in the blog's settings file. The password is stored, not hashed, because the blog needs the real value to connect. Treat this screen like any place that holds a real credential, and limit who can open it.

Mail Server Settings

The outgoing mail server and the sender addresses are used for comment notices, contact messages, password resets, invitations, and error emails. If you change them, send yourself a test message. See Email and Comments.

Blog Options, Step by Step

Open Blog Options. It has a short block of checkboxes at the top and several panels below. Here is what each one does and why you might change it.

The Main Block

  • Use SSL. Check this once your site has a valid certificate. Disqus and some embedded media need SSL to work correctly.
  • Server Rewrite Rule in Place. Check this only after your server hides index.cfm from addresses. The blog builds its links to match, so the box must match the server. See URL Rewrites, Explained.
  • Defer Non-Essential Scripts. Loads some scripts after the page appears, so the first view is faster.
  • Minimize Code. Strips extra whitespace and comments from the main pages before they are sent. It makes pages smaller and faster, at the cost of harder-to-read page source.
  • Send Diagnostics. Emails the blog owner when a new error happens. Error emails show the failing address, the message, and a stack trace, but never form values. Repeated errors are rate-limited, so your inbox is not flooded.
  • Disable Cache. Turns off the page cache. Use it while you change a theme, and turn it off again afterward, because it slows the site for every visitor.

jQuery and Kendo

These settings choose where jQuery loads from, and which Kendo library the blog uses. Check Commercial Kendo UI Edition only if you have licensed Kendo UI and installed it on the server. Otherwise the blog looks for files that are not there. Defer Kendo Commercial on Public Site loads the smaller free library for readers, and loads the larger one only in the admin site.

Logging

Visitor logging records page views for the Visitor Log and the ban tools. Choose how long to keep visitor logs, from one month to six, and how long to keep error and administrative logs, up to two years. Shorter retention means a smaller database.

Analytics and Sharing

Enter your Google Analytics ID and any AddThis settings if you use them. Leave them empty if you do not.

Maps

Paste an Azure Maps key into the Azure Maps panel to embed maps and routes in posts. Without a key, map features do not work. Bing Maps is kept for blogs with an existing Bing Maps account, but new setups should use Azure Maps. See Maps in Posts.

Media and Fallbacks

The media panel holds the image compression default, the image and video size limits, and the No-Image Fallback setting. The fallback decides what a post shows when it has no picture. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Disqus, Greensock, and Other Libraries

The Disqus panel turns on Disqus comments and holds its identifier. See Email and Comments. The Greensock panel is for the animation library, if your theme uses it.

Troubleshooting a Setting That Does Not Take Effect

Some settings apply right away, and some need the application to restart. If a change does not appear, try these in order: reload the page, use Refresh Site in the admin, reinitialize with ?reinit=1 while signed in, and restart the application server as a last step. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • Keep the rewrite box and the server in step. A mismatch produces links that return not-found errors.
  • Turn off Disable Cache when you finish. It is useful while you work, but it makes the site slower for everyone.
  • Do not check Commercial Kendo UI unless you installed it. The site will look for files that are not on the server.

PAGES.TITLE: Email and Comments
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The emails Galaxie Blog sends with your branding, and how to switch comments to Disqus.
PAGES.BODY:
Email is how the blog keeps readers and administrators informed. It sends subscriber mail when you release a post, notifies people when a comment is approved, and reports errors when you turn on diagnostics. This page explains how the email settings work and which emails go out.

What Email the Blog Sends and Why

A blog works best when readers come back. Subscriber email is the simplest way to bring them back, and comment notices let commenters know when a conversation continues. Diagnostic email tells you about problems you might not otherwise see.

The Mail Settings

The mail settings are on the Blog Settings screen. They are:

  • Mail Server, the address of your outgoing mail server.
  • Mail User Name and Mail Password, if your server needs them.
  • Mail Failto Address, where undeliverable mail goes.
  • Blog Email Address, the address emails are sent from.
  • CC Email, an address that receives a copy.

The blog will not send email if the Blog Email Address is blank, and it reports that as an error. Fill it in before you test anything.

Which Emails Go Out

Subscriber Email

When you release a post, the blog asks whether to email subscribers. It only asks when the post is released, has not been emailed before, and is not dated in the future. Choosing yes sends the post to every verified subscriber. The blog remembers that the post was emailed, so it will not send the same post twice. Scheduled releases do not send this email on their own, so check the prompt after a scheduled release goes live.

Comment Notices

When a comment is approved, the blog emails the people who subscribed to that post's comments. The subscribe option appears on the comment form.

Error Diagnostics

If you turn on Send Diagnostics in Blog Options, the blog emails you errors as they happen, rate-limited so a flood of errors does not flood your inbox.

Comment Settings

Each post has an Allow Comments checkbox in the post editor. Turning it off stops new comments on that post. Each comment has a Moderated checkbox, which you can use to mark a comment you have reviewed. When a commenter is not signed in and moderation is on, their comment waits for approval before it appears.

Testing Email

Send yourself a test by subscribing with your own address. The subscription sends a confirmation email, and you must confirm it before the address counts as a subscriber. If the confirmation does not arrive, check the mail server, the sending address, and your spam folder, in that order.

Gotchas

  • A blank Blog Email Address stops all sending. Fill it in first.
  • Scheduled releases do not email subscribers on their own. Check the prompt once the post is live.
  • Subscribers must confirm. An unconfirmed address does not receive post emails.

PAGES.TITLE: URL Rewrites, Explained
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Hiding index.cfm from addresses with a server rewrite rule, and turning on the matching setting in the blog.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can build clean addresses without index.cfm in them, such as /my-post instead of /index.cfm/my-post. That takes two things working together: a setting in the blog, and a rewrite rule on the web server. This page explains both, and why the blog cannot provide the rule itself.

Why Clean Addresses Help Readers and Search Engines

Clean addresses are easier to read, easier to share, and easier for search engines to understand. A link ending in index.cfm works, but it looks like a technical detail leaked into your site. Removing it is a small change with a lasting effect on how your posts look in search results.

The Two Parts

The blog side is a checkbox called Server Rewrite Rule in place? on the Blog Options screen. When it is checked, the blog builds every link without index.cfm, and it strips the filename from the sitemap. The web server side is a rewrite rule that takes a clean address and passes it to the blog. The blog cannot add that rule, because the rule belongs to the web server, not the application.

If you check the box without the server rule, every link on the site will break. If you install the server rule without checking the box, the links will still work, but they will carry index.cfm and the clean form will be unused.

What the Blog Ships With

The blog ships a web.config file at its root. It turns off directory browsing, turns on compression, shows detailed error pages, and adds the file types the blog uses, such as WebP images and caption files. It does not contain any URL rewrite rules. The help text on the Blog Options screen tells you to set the rule on the server yourself.

When the Setting Takes Effect

The setting is read when the application starts. After you change it, restart the application or reinitialize it, so the blog picks up the new value. If links look wrong after a change, that is the first thing to check. The troubleshooting page covers how to reinitialize.

Testing on Your Own Machine

A local test server usually has no rewrite rules. Leave the box unchecked there, so the links use index.cfm and work. Turn it on only where the server rule exists, which is normally your live site.

Gotchas

  • Checking the box without the server rule breaks every link. Set the server rule first.
  • The sitemap follows the same setting. It strips index.cfm only when the box is checked.
  • A change needs a restart or reinitialize before it shows.

PAGES.TITLE: Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: When a change does not show up, how to reinitialize or restart the blog, where the error logs are, and how to see a startup error.
PAGES.BODY:
When something on your blog does not look right, start with the simplest fix. Most problems are a stale cache or code that has not reloaded after a change. This page covers the tools for those cases, and where to find the errors.

Where the Blog Stores Error Logs

  • Error Log in the admin site lists errors the blog caught. Use the Hits column to see which errors repeat.
  • Send Diagnostics in Blog Options emails the blog owner when a new error happens.
  • The galaxieBlogErrors log file on the server records every error, including errors that happen before the blog starts.

Reinitializing

Add ?reinit=1 to any address on your blog, for example https://yourblog.example/index.cfm?reinit=1. It resets the application and clears the caches. Use it after you change settings, or move files on the server.

Reinitializing affects every visitor, so the blog only accepts it from a signed-in administrator. It also works while the blog is not yet installed, or when a reinstall has been requested.

Refresh Site and Reload ORM Objects

The admin home screen has two icons for the same job without a URL: Refresh Site clears the caches, and Reload ORM Objects reloads the database mappings. Both need the Manage Settings capability.

When You Need to Restart

Restart the application server, not just the blog, when you have:

  • moved or deleted files on the server
  • changed a database column or a mapping in the code

Both ColdFusion and Lucee remember old component locations until they restart, and a reinitialize does not always clear them.

Startup Errors

If the blog fails to start, visitors see a generic message. To see the real error, add ?startupDebug=1 to the address. The detail appears only for a signed-in administrator, or while the blog has not finished starting. Otherwise, check the galaxieBlogErrors log on the server.

Pages That Do Not Update

Work through these in order: reinitialize, then Refresh Site, then check the page again. For active theme work, turn on Disable Cache in Blog Options, so each change shows at once.

Gotchas

  • Turn Disable Cache off when you finish. It makes the blog slower for every visitor.
  • Reinitialize when traffic is low, since it resets the blog for everyone who is visiting.

PAGES.TITLE: Search Engines and Feeds
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How readers and search engines find your posts: the RSS feed, the sitemap, clean links, and what is excluded from the feed.
PAGES.BODY:
Search engines find your posts through a sitemap. Readers and feed readers follow your RSS feed. This page explains what the blog provides for each, and where you control them.

How Search Engines Find Your Pages and Posts

A sitemap is a list of every address on your site, with a note for each one. It helps a search engine find new posts quickly, instead of waiting to stumble on them through links. Galaxie Blog generates the sitemap for you, so it stays current as you publish and remove content.

Search engines do more than find pages. They decide what each page is about, and they show a title and short description in the results. Galaxie Blog gives you the controls for most of that:

  • Titles. A post's title is what most search results show first. Write one that says what the post is about, and keep it distinct from your other titles.
  • Descriptions. The Description field is used for cards and search previews, and it can hold up to 1,250 characters. Write a sentence a reader would want to see in a result, not the first paragraph copied over.
  • Addresses. A short, readable address tells both readers and search engines what a page is about. Galaxie Blog builds addresses from the title, and you can change them in the post's Alias window. See Post URLs and Redirects.
  • Links between your pages. Related posts, page collections, and the homepage all link your content together. Search engines follow those links to find and rank everything.
  • Released content only. Posts that are still pending or have been removed are left out of the sitemap, so search engines only see what readers can see.

The Sitemap

The sitemap lists the blog's front page, every post, and every page. It is generated as XML. The blog's robots.txt file points search engines to it, so most crawlers will find it without any setup. If you use Galaxie Blog's clean addresses, the sitemap uses the same clean form. See URL Rewrites, Explained.

Keeping a Test Site Out of Search

A test or staging site should not appear in search results. Galaxie Blog handles this with a setting called Production Site, found under Blog Settings. When it is not checked, every page carries a noindex tag, which tells search engines to skip it. Check the box on your live site, and leave it off everywhere else.

Tag pages carry their own noindex tag, because they repeat content from posts and do not add much to search.

The RSS Feed

Every page links to the RSS feed through a standard tag, so feed readers can discover it. The feed is cached. It accepts two options you can add to its address:

  • mode sets how much of each post appears. full includes the whole post and short includes a summary.
  • mode2 filters the feed by day, by month, or by category.

The feed is RSS 2.0. The blog does not provide an Atom feed, so readers that only accept Atom will need the RSS address.

Pages and Blog Posts in the Feed

Galaxie Blog has two kinds of content, and they behave differently in the RSS feed. Pages are built for evergreen content, such as an about page, a service description, or a guide that stays true for years. They are not meant to change often.

Blog posts are for dated content: news, updates, and anything you write at a particular moment. Posts are what a feed reader expects, so the RSS feed includes blog posts only. A new page does not appear in the feed, even when it is released. You can also leave a single post out of the feed by turning off its display-on-feed setting, which is useful for a post you want on the site but not in readers' inboxes.

The sitemap is different. It lists both pages and posts, so search engines can find evergreen pages as well as new posts.

Verification Tags

The blog does not have a field for Google or Bing site-verification tags. To verify your site with those services, add the verification tag through the Custom Header Script panel in Theme Settings. Google Analytics and the Bing Maps key are separate settings, and neither one verifies your site.

Gotchas

  • Turn on Production Site on the live site. A site without it is marked noindex.
  • There is no Atom feed. Use the RSS address for any reader.
  • Verification tags go in the header script, since there is no dedicated field.

PAGES.TITLE: Media and Maps, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Media and Maps, Start to Finish
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete guide to media in Galaxie Blog: pictures, video, maps, galleries, and the animated backgrounds. It explains what each kind of media does, where to add it, and what the blog does to it once it is uploaded.

Inline Media vs the Main Picture

Media does two different jobs in a post. Some media sits inside the text, such as a picture next to a paragraph. Other media is the post's main picture, the enclosure, which appears at the top of the post and on the card. The blog keeps those two jobs in two places. The body editor handles the inline media, and the Enclosure Editor handles the main picture. That way, a large hero image or a video does not get in the way of your writing.

The Main Picture: The Enclosure

The enclosure is the large picture, video, map, or carousel that opens the post. It is also what readers see on the card, and what gets shared on social media. Set it in the Enclosure Editor. Choose what kind of media to use, then upload, embed, or build it. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

Pictures

Pictures are the most common media. You can add them inline in the body, or as the enclosure. Common web image formats work. When you upload a picture, the blog creates optimized copies for Facebook, Twitter, Google, and the blog's own pages, so each one looks right where it appears. See Adding an Image to a Post and Image Optimization and WebP.

How Social Crops Are Made Automatically

A picture that looks good in a post often looks wrong in a link preview, because each platform wants a different shape. Making those crops by hand is slow and easy to forget. The blog makes them when you upload, so the picture is ready for every place it appears.

Video

You can embed a YouTube or Vimeo video, or upload your own file. Uploaded video can have a cover image and WebVTT captions. See Video in a Post.

Maps and Routes

Maps use Azure Maps, so the first step is an Azure Maps key in Blog Options. Once the key is in place, you can insert a map, or a route with two or more stops, from the editor. On cards, a map shows as a static picture, which keeps listing pages fast. The full map appears on the post. See Maps in Posts.

Why Cards Show a Still Map

A card page can show many posts at once. A live map on each card would load many interactive maps, and most of them would never be touched. A static picture gives the reader the location at a glance, and the live map waits for the post itself.

Galleries and Carousels

When you have several pictures to show together, use a gallery, where readers click through the thumbnails, or a carousel, which rotates through the pictures on its own. See Galleries and Carousels.

Animated Backgrounds

A post can open with a live animated background instead of a picture. The animation plays on the post's own page, on desktop. Cards and phones show a static gradient, so the listing pages stay fast. See Animated Heroes with Vanta.

When a Post Has No Picture

Not every post needs a picture. The No-Image Fallback setting decides what a post shows instead: a plain placeholder, a generated gradient, a photo from your pool, or nothing. The fallback is set once for the whole blog, and it applies to every post without a picture. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Size Limits

Large uploads can fail. The limits for images and videos are set in Blog Options, and the defaults allow typical photos and short videos. For a very large video, hosting it yourself and linking to it is often easier. Check the limits before a big upload, so the failure does not happen halfway through.

Gotchas

  • The enclosure is the card picture. Check the card after you change it, not only the post.
  • Maps need the Azure Maps key. Without it, the map features do not work.
  • A gradient or animation replaces the enclosure. Choosing one removes the picture, so you cannot show both.

PAGES.TITLE: Maps in Posts
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Adding an Azure Maps key, embedding a map or a driving route in a post, and how map previews appear on cards.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can place a map or a route inside a post. Maps use Azure Maps, so the first step is connecting your own Azure Maps key. This page explains why the key is needed, how to add a map or a route, and how the blog shows maps on listing pages.

What the Azure Maps Key Pays For

The map data and the route calculations come from Microsoft's Azure Maps service. Azure requires an account and a key for every request, so the blog cannot provide one for you. Your key identifies your account, and it lets you control your own usage and cost. Enter the key in Blog Options, in the field labeled Azure Maps API Key. Without it, the map features will not work.

Adding a Map

In the post editor, open the Insert menu and choose Map. The map window lets you set the location and the zoom level, and choose a style. The styles are road, grayscale dark, night, road with shaded relief, satellite, and satellite with road labels. The zoom level is saved as a whole number, so small changes are rounded.

Adding a Route

Choose Map Directions from the Insert menu to build a route. You choose a travel mode, which is car by default, or bicycle, bus, motorcycle, or pedestrian. Then you enter the stops along the route. The form holds up to sixteen stops, and two is the minimum. Pick a route style the same way you pick a map style.

The route follows the road between the stops, using the travel mode you picked. The live map on the post and the card picture both draw that same road path.

How a Map Appears

A map placed in the body of a post appears where you put it, in a frame about 768 pixels wide and 432 pixels tall.

A map saved as the post's main picture, the enclosure, is shown at the top of the post. Saving a map or a route as the enclosure removes any picture, video, or carousel the post had, because a post has only one enclosure. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

Why Cards Use Still Map Images

A listing page can show many posts at once. A live, interactive map on every card would load a large number of maps, most of which no reader would touch. Galaxie Blog instead fetches a single still image of the map, road path included, the first time it is needed, and saves it on your server. Every card then uses that saved image, so listing pages stay fast. The live map appears only on the post itself.

If the still image cannot be fetched, the blog removes the partial file and tries again later. A missing still image usually means the key is wrong or the service could not be reached.

A Good Way to Use Maps

  • Use a map to show a place a reader needs to find, such as an office or a trailhead.
  • Use a route for a trip with a clear order of stops.
  • Choose a style that stays readable at small sizes, since the card picture is small.

Gotchas

  • No key, no map. Enter the Azure Maps key in Blog Options first.
  • A route follows the road for the travel mode you chose. Change the travel mode to change the path, then check the card picture, since it is saved once and rebuilt after the route is saved.
  • Saving a map as the enclosure removes the picture. Save the picture somewhere else in the post if you want to keep it.

PAGES.TITLE: Image Optimization and WebP
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The automatic crops every uploaded image gets, the compression slider, video upload size, and how WebP is used when the server supports it.
PAGES.BODY:
Every picture you upload is processed before it appears on your site. The blog makes copies sized for each place a picture appears, and it can save them in WebP, a format that loads faster. This page explains why each step exists and what you control.

What Happens to Each Picture You Upload

A photo straight from a camera is often several megabytes, far larger than a web page needs. Sending that to every reader slows the page and wastes their data. Processing the picture once, at upload, means readers download a file sized for the screen they are using.

What You Can Upload

The blog accepts JPEG, GIF, PNG, and WebP pictures. Each file can be up to 25 megabytes. The upload screens show a cropping tool, so you can frame a picture before it is saved. If a file is too large, the blog rejects it after upload, so check the size first. Your server's own limit on the size of a form post also applies, which is why the blog's help text mentions it.

The Copies the Blog Makes

Each picture you use as a post's main picture gets several copies, sized for where it will appear:

  • A thumbnail for admin lists and small previews.
  • Facebook copies for shared links, in the shared size and the link sizes.
  • Twitter copies for large and small link cards.
  • Google copies in 16:9, 4:3, and square shapes, for search results.
  • Pinterest copy, made only when the original is large enough to fill it.
  • Classic copy, a standard 4:3 image used as a fallback.

Each social network wants a different shape, so one picture is never right everywhere. Making these copies by hand takes time and is easy to forget. The blog makes them for you, so a shared link looks right on every platform.

WebP

WebP is a modern format that is smaller than JPEG at the same quality. Where your server can create WebP files, the blog saves WebP copies of the social sizes too. Lucee can always do this. ColdFusion can do it on the 2025 release and later. If your server cannot create WebP, the blog offers a tool to swap in a WebP version you prepared yourself.

Quality

Quality controls the trade-off between file size and sharpness. The site-wide default is set in Blog Options under Default Image Quality, and it ranges from 0.1 to 1.0, with a default of 0.8. Each upload has its own slider, labeled Image Quality (smaller file to higher quality), which starts at the site default. Quality is applied to JPEG and WebP files. A lower setting makes a smaller file, and a higher one keeps more detail.

The default of 0.8 is a good balance for most photos. Raise it for detailed images such as screenshots of text, and lower it for large photos where size matters more than fine detail.

Thumbnails and Caching

Thumbnails are 235 pixels wide and 138 pixels tall. Like the other copies, they are generated once at upload. Because the copies are files on your server, they are served directly, and that is what makes them fast.

Gotchas

  • Pictures over 25 megabytes are rejected. Resize them before upload.
  • The Pinterest copy is skipped for small originals. That is expected, not a failure.
  • Raising quality makes files larger. Set the default with your readers' connections in mind.

PAGES.TITLE: Fallbacks and Hero Pictures
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What a post shows when it has no photo: the four fallback modes, the hero image pool, and the hero cover image.
PAGES.BODY:
Not every post has a picture, and a post without one can look empty in a list. The No-Image Fallback setting decides what a post shows in its picture spot when it has no picture of its own. This page explains the choices and why each one exists.

What Readers See When a Post Has No Picture

A listing of cards looks uneven when some cards have a picture and some have a blank space. A fallback fills that gap with something deliberate. It is also what appears when you share a post that has no picture, so a fallback shapes how your posts look on social networks too.

The Options

The setting is labeled No-Image Fallback on the Blog Options screen. It has five choices:

  • Generic shows the standard placeholder picture. This is the default.
  • Generated creates a gradient for each post as an SVG image file, drawn in the blog's theme colors. The file is made once and saved on your server. Each post gets its own, so the listing does not look repetitive.
  • Pool Photo picks a photo from a pool you supply. The same post always gets the same photo, so a reader who returns sees no change.
  • Animated Background shows a live animation on the post's own page only. Listings and phones show a still image instead. See Animated Heroes with Vanta.
  • None leaves the picture area empty.

The Pool

The pool option has two settings. Pool Display chooses between a rotating carousel and a single picture. Pool Image Count sets how many pictures the carousel shows. The pool holds up to 75 pictures. Because each post picks by its own ID, the choice is steady, not random.

The Hero Cover Image

A post can have a hero cover image: a single photo you upload for the post that does not replace its live animation or gradient. It shows on listing cards, in the admin list, and as the picture shared on social networks. On the post's own page, a gradient or an animation still plays as chosen. This lets you show a real picture on cards while keeping the live look on the post itself.

How the Choices Are Ranked

When a post is displayed, the blog checks its picture sources in order. A real picture, video, map, or carousel comes first. A chosen gradient or animation comes next. The hero cover image is used on cards and in shares. If none of those exist, the No-Image Fallback applies.

A Good Default

For most blogs, the generated gradients give the best result without any work. They look intentional, they cost nothing to produce, and every post looks different. Use the pool when you have a photo style you want to repeat, and use none only when you prefer a text-only list.

Gotchas

  • The generated gradients are SVG image files, saved on your server, not live CSS, even though the option label mentions CSS.
  • The animation shows only on the post's own page, on desktop. Listings never show it.
  • A chosen gradient or animation replaces the post's picture enclosure. You cannot show both.

PAGES.TITLE: Animated Heroes with Vanta
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to choose an animated Vanta background for a post or the whole site, and when the animation runs.
PAGES.BODY:
An animated hero is a live, moving background at the top of a post. It plays on the post's own page on a desktop, and gives a post a look no still picture can. This page explains what the animation is, why it is limited to the post page, and how to choose one.

Why Animations Play Only on Post Pages

An animation runs continuously and uses the processor. A listing with many animations would slow down every reader and drain phone batteries. So the blog plays the animation only on a single post, on a desktop. Listings, cards, and phones show a still image instead. The post itself gets the full effect, and everything else stays fast.

The Effects

The Effect menu offers nine choices: Birds, Clouds, Clouds 2, Fog, Globe, Net, Rings, Waves, and Random. Random is meant to pick one per post. Check the result on the post's own page before you rely on it, because the Random choice does not always resolve to an effect the way the other choices do.

Adjusting an Effect

Each effect has its own options. The Speed slider runs from 0.3 to 3, with 1 as the normal speed. Most effects let you set colors with swatches, and a set of numeric sliders controls shape and density. For Net and Globe, a Show Dots checkbox adds points to the lines. Mouse, touch, and gyroscope control is turned off, so the animation plays on its own.

Choosing One

Pick an effect whose colors match the post's theme, and keep the speed slow. A fast animation can pull attention from the words. Set the effect in the post's hero window, and check the post on a desktop before you release it.

What the Animation Replaces

Choosing an animation removes the post's picture, video, map, carousel, and gradient, because a post has only one main picture. If you want a picture on cards while keeping the animation on the post, use the hero cover image described in Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

A Site-Wide Default

Blog Options has an Animation Effect setting that applies to posts that have no animation of their own, when the No-Image Fallback is set to Animated Background. It also plays only on the post page.

Gotchas

  • Listings show a still image, not the animation. That is by design.
  • Phones do not play the animation. Check the desktop view when you judge the effect.
  • Choosing an animation removes the picture enclosure. Use the hero cover image to keep a picture on cards.
  • Random may not resolve as expected. Verify it on the post before you release.

Built With

The animations use Vanta.js, which draws on three.js. Both are MIT licensed. See Software and Licenses.

The author's own blog runs on Galaxie Blog at gregoryalexander.com/blog/, which is one place to see these features in use.

PAGES.TITLE: Enclosures: What a Post Shows First
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What an enclosure is, how to add or replace one in the Enclosure Editor, and the order a post uses to choose its main picture.
PAGES.BODY:
A post's enclosure is the main thing it shows first: a picture, a video, a map, a carousel, a gradient, or an animation. Only one can be the enclosure at a time. This page explains why, how the blog chooses what to show, and what each choice removes.

Why a Post Has One Main Picture

A post opens with one strong visual, the thing a reader sees before the words. Showing two competing headers would confuse the page, and a card in a list has only one place for a picture. Limiting a post to one enclosure keeps the top of every post clear, and it means the card and the post always agree.

The Types

  • An image you uploaded.
  • A video, either one you uploaded or a YouTube or Vimeo link.
  • A map or a route.
  • A carousel of images that rotates.
  • A gradient, a color background you choose.
  • An animation, a live background on the post page.

How the Blog Chooses What to Show

On the post's own page, the blog checks the enclosure in a fixed order. A picture, video, or carousel comes first, then a map, then a gradient, then an animation. Because saving one type clears the others, a post normally holds only one of them at a time, so the order rarely matters. If none is set, the blog uses the No-Image Fallback.

Listing pages and admin thumbnails use their own order, and they add the hero cover image as well. That is why a card can show a different picture from the one at the top of the post, if you set a hero cover image.

What Each Choice Removes

Choosing a type clears the others that conflict with it:

  • An image or video clears any map or carousel.
  • A map clears the picture, video, and carousel.
  • A carousel clears the picture, video, and map.
  • A gradient clears the picture, video, map, carousel, and any animation.
  • An animation clears the picture, video, map, carousel, and any gradient.

The hero cover image clears nothing, which is why it can sit alongside any of these.

How to Choose Well

  1. Pick the picture that best represents the post, since it also appears on cards and in shares.
  2. Check the card on the front page after you save. A picture that looks good at the top of the post can crop badly on a card.
  3. Use the hero cover image when you want a real picture on cards but the live look on the post.

Gotchas

  • Saving a new enclosure removes the old one. Save a copy of anything you may want back.
  • The enclosure is the card and share picture. Check the card after you change it.
  • A gradient or animation replaces the picture. You cannot show both at the top of the post.
